sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: A warm front will lift north into British Columbia tonight, while a cold front stalls offshore Wednesday and into Thursday. Additional weather systems will move through Friday through Sunday for more lowland rain and gusty winds. After a brief break Monday, another front will arrive on Tuesday.

sections.title: Short term (tonight through Thursday night)
paragraphs: Western WA remains under strong and moist SW flow with rain and high elevation snow across the region. The warm front will lift north into B.C tonight and the interior will see a break in the precipitation. Wetter conditions will remain along the coast and Olympics through Wednesday as the cold front stalls offshore. Wednesday will be mild in the warm sector with temperatures in the 60s.

Several weather headlines are in place with the main impact being strong winds along the coast and North Interior. Expect south winds of 20 to 30 MPH with gusts to 50 MPH. Winds will ease Wednesday afternoon. In addition, there's potential for large waves crashing along the coast leading to a High Surf Advisory. Minor coastal flooding is also possible near Wednesday morning's high tide in the San Juans and western Whatcom County. Lastly, due to heavy precipitation, the Skokomish River in Mason County is seeing sharp rises with Minor flooding possible.

The cold front will continue to stall and weaken offshore moving into Thursday. The coast and Olympics may see periods of light rain but the interior and Cascades will see a brief break. There's more active weather starting Thursday night. 33

sections.title: Long term (Friday through Tuesday)
paragraphs: From Thursday night into Friday, there's another strong Pacific storm system moving in for more lowland rain, high elevation mountain snow, and gusty winds. Winds will be the strongest along the coast where the probability of seeing gusts of 50 MPH is 70-80 percent. It will be windy in the interior as well with gusts to 30-40 MPH. This system will weaken as it moves inland on Saturday. We will then see a second system track through on Sunday for more wind and rain. Additional rainfall will keep the Skokomish River running high with the possibility of river flooding. These systems will generate large waves with the potential for High Surf and beach erosion along the Pacific coast. Minor coastal flooding will also need to monitored around the time of high tides across the Salish Sea.
Moving forward, there appears to be a brief break in the pattern on Monday. By Tuesday we see more breezy winds and rain as the next front moves in. 33

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: A mixed bag of ceilings this afternoon as ongoing showers are keeping conditions messy through the interior. Most areas are seeing MVFR/IFR in showers along with low ceilings and low visibilities (3-6SM). Ceilings should slowly, and gradually improve towards low-end VFR late this evening as rain begins to dissipate. S/SE winds will remain breezy this afternoon, with gusts up to 20 to 25 kts possible. Areas along the coast and especially terminals in the north interior (KBLI) could see gusts up to 30 kts tonight. Winds will remain elevated Wednesday morning, easing by the afternoon. Ceilings should remain VFR on Wednesday morning.

KSEA...MVFR/IFR conditions this afternoon in showers. Low visibilities (2-4SM) will likely continue in showers through the early evening hours, before conditions start to ease up into VFR. S/E winds 8 to 12 knots this afternoon, moving towards more of a 5 to 10 knots later this evening and into the overnight hours. VFR conditions Wednesday morning.
Mazurkiewicz

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Winds will continue to increase over the area waters this afternoon, peaking this evening and remaining elevated throughout the overnight hours. A Gale Warning remains in effect for the coastal waters until Wednesday evening as these wind speeds persist. A Gale Warning is also in effect for the East Strait of Juan De Fuca, along with the Northern Inland Waters. Elsewhere, A Small Craft Advisory will continue for Admiralty Inlet and the West Entrance of the Strait until Wednesday evening when winds will start to ease across the whole region.
Seas this afternoon generally around 16 to 18 feet this afternoon, remaining high through Wednesday morning. Seas will ease towards more of a 12 to 14 feet on Thursday.

Another strong low pressure system will start to move towards the coastal waters late Thursday night into Friday, bringing stronger winds and higher waves. Latest guidance still suggests a 60-70% chance of storm force wind gusts over the coastal waters. Winds may ease slightly Friday night before another round of strong winds arrives on the coastal waters, with a 30-40% chance of storm force gusts over the waters. Winds will slowly ease late night Sunday as these systems move away from the area.

Additionally, guidance suggests building large waves over the coast, generally above 20 feet starting on Friday afternoon. GEFS and ECMWF probabilities continuously has shown a 20-30% chance of seas above 25 feet heading into late Friday into early Saturday morning. Subtle shifts in the low pressure may change waves and where the largest waves generate, with seas nearing 30 ft not out of the equation, especially near the southern portions of the waters.
Mazurkiewicz

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: After a storm system clips the area today, expect drier weather Wednesday and Thursday before another storm system brings widespread rain and breezy conditions to the area Friday into the weekend. Sneaker waves will be a threat through the week with another round of high surf conditions appearing increasingly likely Saturday. A cool and wet pattern continues early next week.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Now through Monday...Radar imagery and surface observations as of early Tuesday afternoon depicts a band of rain over far northwest Oregon and southwest Washington as an atmospheric river pushes into the Pacific Northwest and British Columbia. Moisture that is being squeezed between upper-level troughing over the Gulf of Alaska and upper-level ridging over the Great Basin and southwestern U.S. has become an atmospheric river aimed towards our area. High pressure to our south is resulting in a pretty distinct line between rain and dry conditions. Most of the rain over the past 12 hours has been north of a line from Newport, OR to The Dalles, OR. Surface observations have shown rain amounts between 0-0.10" for locations along this line and southward, while areas to the north have received anywhere from 0.25 to 1 inch in the last 12 hours. The heaviest rain amounts have been further north over the Olympic Peninsula. Breezy southerly winds continue along the coast through this afternoon with gusts to 30-40 mph. Inland, winds are generally coming out of the southeast but remaining under 10 mph. Tonight, upper-level ridging will build over the area, gradually decreasing rain and returning drier conditions.

Upper-level ridging will reach its peak amplitude on Wednesday, supporting dry and unseasonably warm temperatures across interior valleys with high temperatures forecast in the mid to upper 60s. Daily record high temperatures could be broken tomorrow, including the 64F record at Portland (PDX) and Hillsboro (HIO) set in 1989, and 66F at Vancouver (VUO) set in 1904, 1907, and 1930 may be in jeopardy. However, a 20-40% chance for showers will continue in Pacific County and along the coast north of Tillamook. Thursday is also looking to be a mostly dry day with similar chances for showers along the north Oregon and south Washington coast. Daytime temperatures will lower a few degrees, though will still be unseasonably warm in the low 60s across interior valleys. By Thursday night, upper- level ridging will begin to shift eastward as upper-level troughing begins pushing into the northeast Pacific.

There is high confidence that a deep upper-level trough will become situated over the northeast Pacific west of Canada from late Thursday/Friday into the weekend, returning troughing to the Pacific Northwest. Multiple surface frontal systems are expected to move through the region during this time, bringing repeated chances for widespread rain and breezy winds. There is still uncertainty with specific rainfall amounts and peak wind gusts; however, we can say for certain that it will be wet. This is shaping up to be another atmospheric river event as long- range ensembles indicate a 60-70% chance for vapor transport to exceed 500 kg/(ms) at the leading edge of this trough on Friday somewhere along the Oregon coast with similar probabilities of vapor transport values remaining above 250 kg/(ms) into Sunday. Increasingly saturated soils from multiple weather systems could allow for greater runoff into area rivers, meaning at least isolated flooding cannot be ruled out. However, chances for widespread flooding of rivers remains <5% at this time. It's still too far out to determine hourly rainfall rates, but if rain is heavy enough, we could also see some urban and small stream flooding of low-lying and poor drainage areas. People should make sure to clear gutters and storm drains of any leaves or debris.

Across the Cascades, it appears that this system will be warm enough to keep snow levels between 5500-6500 feet on Friday, keeping the passes snow-free. By Saturday, snow levels drop to around 5000 ft, potentially bringing some light snow to Willamette Pass. From Friday afternoon to Sunday afternoon, there is a 30% chance for total snowfall amounts of 1 inch or greater along Santiam and Willamette Passes, and a 10% chance along Highway 26 at Government Camp. Much higher snowfall amounts expected above 6000-6500 feet.

When it comes to winds, there is a 20-40% chance for maximum wind gusts exceeding 55 mph along the coast Friday and Saturday, with the highest chances on Friday. Wind gusts of this magnitude could result in scattered or widespread power outages or tree damage. Along the I-5 corridor, there is a 5-15% chance for maximum wind gusts exceeding 40 mph, which could result in isolated power outages or tree damage. To prepare, make sure to secure loose outdoor items.
Heading into early next week, the vast majority of ensemble members show some degree of troughing over the West Coast, maintaining a generally cool and wet pattern.     -10/03

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 00Z Thursday...A warm front has shifted northward into Washington late this afternoon and evening where most of the rain has now shifted. South of the warm front, conditions have trended VFR except along portions of the coast, which are still stuck in IFR conditions. Elsewhere skies have mostly cleared or at least clouds have thinned. With light winds and dewpoints in the mid 50s, and models suggesting only passing high clouds overnight, it seems the probability for fog development is growing rapidly, particularly along and west of Interstate 5. Despite only 10-20% of the high resolution ensembles suggesting fog development in the Willamette Valley, have opted to include it in the TAFs for KEUG, KSLE, KUAO and KHIO for now. May need to add IFR conditions into KPDX, but low level easterly winds should help to keep conditions VFR. Fog and low clouds will be more stubborn than normal to scatter out on Wednesday, particularly across the western and southern portions of the Willamette Valley given weak pressure gradients and winds aloft so will not be surprised if some sites stay stuck in IFR conditions into Wednesday evening. Meanwhile, gusty southerly winds along the coast will continue through the taf period with gusts generally hovering between 20-30 kt.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...A warm front has lifted north of the region with thinning cloud cover over the terminal. Easterly winds continue at the surface, which should help to keep conditions VFR overnight. With that said, not super confident we won't see those winds weaken with fog either developing or pushing upriver into the terminal as a result. For now will plan to keep the TAF VFR, but will be monitoring trends to see if any adjustments towards IFR conditions is needed.

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: A frontal boundary draped across the waters is supporting hazardous conditions to some degree for all zones. Currently, a Gale Warning is in effect for waters north of Cape Falcon, including the Columbia River Bar while Hazardous Seas Warnings are in place south of Cape Falcon to Florence. The Gale Warning expands southward to zones PZZ272 and PZZ252 later this evening. Wind gusts around 40 kt are expected through Wednesday afternoon before headlines transition to Hazardous Seas Warnings for all zones. A building west swell will increase seas to 14-17 ft around 14 seconds through Wednesday. Hazardous Seas conditions are expected to continue through Wednesday night before possibly dropping down to Small Craft Advisory conditions.

A brief lull in activity is expected on Thursday before ramping back up late Thursday evening. Another strong front is expected to move into the waters, likely bringing at least Gales with a 70-80% chance and a 10-30% chance for Storms (highest in the outer waters). Seas are again expected to rise above 20 ft by Friday afternoon with a 30-50% chance for greater than 25 ft and a 10-15% chance for 30 ft or greater in the outer waters. Another strong front is expected during the latter half of Saturday, continuing the active pattern for the waters.   -19

sections.title: Beach hazards
paragraphs: A moderate to high sneaker wave threat continues along the coast through this week as a westerly swell of 10-12 ft at 13-15 seconds increases to 14-16 ft midweek. This will result in waves running up significantly farther on a beach than normal, including over rocks and jetties. Sneaker waves can suddenly knock people off of their feet and quickly pull them into the frigid ocean which may lead to serious injury or drowning.
There is also the potential for tidal overflow flooding Wednesday as the tide plus anomaly are forecasted between 10 and 11 ft (MLLW). This could lead to further water inundation and coastal erosion.

Additionally, confidence is increasing that a stronger westerly swell of 20-24 ft with a dominant period at 16-18 seconds will impact the coast on Saturday for dangerous surf conditions. Destructive waves may wash over beaches, jetties, and other structures unexpectedly.

Extreme caution should be used if you plan to visit beaches this week. The large wave runup may dislodge logs on area beaches and result in them rolling up and down area beaches, which have historically killed or seriously injured unsuspecting people, so there will be much more of a threat than just getting wet from a rogue wave.       -03
